title: When the Event happens, it simply happens.
subtitle: The surah opens on a certainty, not a maybe

row.title: when it comes
sub: a fact with a fixed time

then: The Makkan listeners found resurrection unbelievable and treated it as imagination. The surah does not open with an argument. It opens with {idea}When the Occurrence occurs{/idea}, a name for the Day chosen, Ibn Kathir says, because it is real and will surely come.
now: You plan in years: the mortgage, the retirement age, the kids' graduation. Death and the Day sit in a mental folder marked {trap}someday, maybe{/trap}. This verse moves them to the folder marked {idea}certain{/idea}.
old: The Day is something to think about later, if at all.
new: The Day is the one appointment in my calendar that cannot be moved.
try: Tonight before sleep, say one sentence to yourself about the Day as a fact, not a maybe.

title: When it comes, nobody will call it fake.
subtitle: No one can deny it, stop it, or take it back
then: In Makkah, denying the resurrection was easy talk. Ibn Kathir explains that once Allah commands the Day to begin, {idea}none can stop it or prevent it{/idea}. Qatadah said it will not be discontinued, taken back, or aborted.
now: Online, any fact can be called fake. You can scroll past, mute, block, unfollow. There is always another opinion. {trap}Denial works well, right up until the thing arrives.{/trap} That Day, nobody posts a counter-argument.
old: If I do not believe it, it does not really apply to me.
new: My doubt does not delay it by one second, so my preparation should not wait either.
try: Pick one thing you keep postponing because the Day feels unreal, and do a small part of it today.

title: The Day lowers some people and lifts others.
subtitle: Rank here is not rank there
then: Al-Hasan and Qatadah explained it: the Day {trap}lowers some to the lowest places, even if they were mighty in this life{/trap}, and {reward}raises others to the highest grades, even if they were weak{/reward}. In Makkah, tribal rank decided almost everything.
now: At work there is a clear ladder: the corner office, the intern, the cleaner who comes in after everyone leaves. You know where you stand on it. {idea}The Day uses a different ladder{/idea}, and people may swap places.
old: People's importance is roughly what it looks like from outside.
new: The quiet person I overlook may stand far above me that Day.
try: Thank one person today, by name, whose work usually goes unnoticed.

title: The ground you trust will shake like a sieve.
subtitle: The most stable thing you know becomes unstable

row.title: only Allah holds
sub: even the earth moves on command

then: Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and others said the earth will be {trap}violently shaken{/trap}, over all its surface and through its depths. Ar-Rabi bin Anas compared it to a sifter shaken with everything in it.
now: You have built your life on things that feel like solid ground: the job contract, the house, your health. Then one phone call or one scan result, and the floor moves. {idea}That small shake is a preview of what is not permanent.{/idea}
old: Some things in my life are simply stable and safe.
new: Even the ground under my feet holds only because Allah holds it.
try: The next time you feel your feet on the floor, say quietly: only You are permanent.

title: Even the mountains get ground down.
subtitle: The biggest thing you know is not permanent
then: To the Arabs, mountains were the picture of permanence. The tafsir says they will be {trap}relentlessly pulverized{/trap}. Ibn Zayd linked it to another verse that describes them as a heap of sand poured out.
now: The big company that seemed untouchable. The family name everyone respected. The career you thought was set for life. {trap}Things you called mountains{/trap} can fold in a year. {idea}What you did for Allah keeps its shape.{/idea}
old: If something is big and old enough, it will always be there.
new: If mountains crumble, my biggest worries and my biggest securities are both temporary.
try: Write down one thing that feels like a mountain to you right now. Under it, write: this too is temporary.

title: Mountains end as dust in the wind.
subtitle: Scattered, then gone without a trace
then: Ali described it as {trap}a rising dust storm that soon fades, leaving no trace{/trap}. Ibn Abbas likened it to embers rising from a fire that go out as soon as they land. Something huge becomes nothing at all.
now: Dust in a sunbeam through the window. You watch it float, then it is gone. Your trophies, your old profiles, the arguments you were so sure you had to win. {idea}A lot of it will end like that dust.{/idea}
old: The things I worked hardest for will leave a mark.
new: What looks heavy now can end as dust, so I should weigh what I chase.
try: Next time you see dust in sunlight, ask: will what I am doing today outlast this?

title: On that Day, everyone falls into one of three groups.
subtitle: Humanity sorted into three, not two
then: Ibn Kathir explains the three: those on the right, given their records in their right hands; those on the left, given theirs in the left; and {reward}the foremost, nearest to Allah{/reward}, fewer in number. He notes the end of the surah shows the same three at death.
now: Life sorts people all the time: grade bands, salary tiers, credit scores. You know how to move between them with effort. {idea}This sorting is already in progress{/idea}, one prayer, one kind word, one lie at a time.
old: I'm a decent person, so I will land on the good side somehow.
new: The sorting is happening in my ordinary choices, today.
try: Ask yourself honestly which group your last 24 hours point to. Then do one thing that points higher.

title: The people of the right: what a place to be!
subtitle: A question meant to make you long for it
then: The verse names the group and then asks about them, a way of saying {reward}how fortunate they are{/reward}. The tafsir says they are given their records in their right hands, and As-Suddi said they make up most of the people of Paradise.
now: You open an exam result and see the word that means you passed. Your shoulders drop and you call your mother. {reward}Being handed your record in your right hand{/reward} is that feeling, with no fear left.
old: Being among the right means barely scraping through.
new: The right is a place of honor, not a lucky escape.
try: Make a short dua today: O Allah, make me one of the people of the right.

title: The people of the left: how sad their state!
subtitle: The same question, with the opposite weight
then: The same form of question, now for those on the left, who receive their records in their left hands. Ibn Kathir calls them the people of the Fire and adds a short prayer: {trap}may Allah save us from their actions{/trap}. He prays against the deeds, not only the destination.
now: You see where a habit leads in someone else: the uncle and his temper, the friend and the debts. You know how it ends. {idea}The prayer is to be saved from the habits, while there is time to drop them.{/idea}
old: The left side is for other, worse people.
new: The road to the left is made of actions, and I can step off any of them.
try: Name one habit you would not want written in your record. Skip it once today.

title: Those who rushed ahead here are ahead there.
subtitle: The foremost in good stay foremost on the Day
then: Ibn Kathir says the foremost rank above those on the right and include {reward}the Messengers, Prophets, true believers and martyrs{/reward}. He links them to another verse about those foremost in good deeds by Allah's leave. The doubled word says it: first here, first there.
now: The group chat asks who can help someone move flat on Saturday. Someone always types me first, before thinking of excuses. {idea}That speed toward good{/idea} is what this verse honors.
old: I will get to good deeds once things settle down.
new: Being early to good is itself the rank.
try: The next time a chance to help comes up today, say yes first and work out the details after.

title: Their reward is to be brought near.
subtitle: Nearness to Allah is named before any garden
then: After naming the foremost, the verse gives their title before any garden is described: {reward}the ones brought near{/reward}. Ibn Kathir says they are in a better grade and nearer to Allah than those on the right.
now: You know the difference between a gift card from your manager and an hour where they really listen to you. One is nice. {idea}The other is being close.{/idea} The verse names closeness first.
old: Paradise is mainly about what I will get.
new: The greatest part is whom I will be near.
try: Spend two quiet minutes in sujood today asking only to be near Allah, nothing else.

title: Their home is the Gardens of Delight.
subtitle: Nearness comes with a place to live

row.title: the gardens
sub: the home that goes with it

then: The verses move from who the foremost are, to what they are, to where they live: {reward}the Gardens of Delight{/reward}. For listeners in the dry valley of Makkah, a garden was a picture of everything good.
now: After a long shift you come home, kick off your shoes, and the house is warm. That is the feeling of arriving. {reward}The Gardens of Delight{/reward} are the arrival after a life of striving.
old: My effort now leads to an uncertain end.
new: Effort toward Allah ends in a home, not in nothing.
try: When you get home today, pause at the door and ask Allah for a home in the Gardens of Delight.

title: Many of the foremost come from the early generations.
subtitle: The first believers set the pace
then: Scholars differed. Some said the earlier ones are earlier nations. Ibn Kathir preferred {idea}the earlier generations of this Ummah{/idea}, citing the Prophet's ﷺ words that the best people are his generation, then the next, then the next.
now: You read about people who believed when it cost them family and safety. Your faith costs you an early alarm. {idea}They set the pace{/idea}, and the door they walked through is still open.
old: The great believers lived back then. That race is over.
new: Their example is a pace to follow, not a closed chapter.
try: Read one short story about an early Muslim today and take one habit from it.

title: Only a few of the foremost come later.
subtitle: Being first to good gets rarer, so it counts more
then: Ibn Kathir explains the later ones as {idea}the later generations of this Ummah{/idea}. Among them, the foremost are {trap}few{/trap}. Abu Hurayrah reported that this news was hard for the Companions when it was revealed.
now: In a packed stadium, a few people still stand up at the back to pray when the time comes. Few is not zero. {idea}A few means there is a place, and someone will take it.{/idea}
old: If only a few make it to the front, it won't be someone like me.
new: A few will be from the later ones, and I can aim to be one of them.
try: Choose one good deed most people around you skip, and do it quietly today.

title: They rest on thrones woven with gold.
subtitle: Rest after a life of standing up
then: Ibn Abbas, and many after him, said these thrones are {reward}woven with gold{/reward}. The listeners knew the honor of a raised seat among chiefs. Here every one of the foremost has one.
now: You stand on the train, stand at the counter, stand in the prayer row at night when you would rather sleep. Your legs ache. {reward}A throne woven with gold{/reward} waits for the one who keeps standing.
old: Tiredness from worship is just tiredness.
new: Every tired moment for Allah is building a seat of rest.
try: Pray two extra rakat tonight and think of that throne while your legs feel it.

title: No one sits in the back row there.
subtitle: Reclining, face to face, everyone included
then: Ibn Kathir says they {reward}face each other, and none of them will be in the back lines{/reward}. In a society where your seat showed your rank, this is a picture of honored friends with no one pushed behind.
now: The wedding where you got the table by the kitchen door. The meeting where your name was left off the invite. {trap}The back row stings.{/trap} {reward}There, every face turns toward every other face.{/reward}
old: There will always be an inner circle, and I'll be outside it.
new: Among the people of Paradise there is no back row.
try: At your next gathering, find the person sitting alone and turn your chair toward them.

title: Servants who never grow old go around them.
subtitle: Service that never tires or changes
then: Ibn Kathir explains these servants as boys {reward}who will never grow up, get old, or change in shape{/reward}. In this life, everything and everyone that serves you wears out. There, nothing does.
now: You care for your parents now the way they once cared for you. You watch them slow down, and you notice yourself slowing too. {idea}Everything here tires.{/idea} The verse points to a place where nothing wears out.
old: Everything good eventually fades and gets old.
new: There is a place where good things do not age.
try: Do one small service for an older family member today without being asked.

title: Their cups are filled from a spring that never runs dry.
subtitle: A drink that never reaches its last drop
then: Ibn Kathir describes cups, jugs and glasses, all filled {reward}from a flowing spring, not from containers that might get empty{/reward}. Every good thing in this life has a last drop. This one has none.
now: The last slice of cake. The final evening of a holiday. The days before payday. {trap}You always feel the end coming.{/trap} {reward}A spring that never stops{/reward} is joy without a countdown.
old: Every good thing I enjoy is already running out.
new: The joys Allah promises have no countdown.
try: Drink your next glass of water slowly, and say alhamdulillah for a supply that has not run out yet.

title: All of the joy, none of the harm.
subtitle: A drink that leaves the mind clear
then: Ibn Abbas said the wine of this life has side effects: it intoxicates, gives headaches, and makes people sick. Allah describes the drink of Paradise {reward}free of all of these{/reward}. The scholars said it does not change their reasoning at all.
now: The late-night binge, the sugar crash, the scrolling that leaves your head foggy at 2 a.m. {trap}So many pleasures here come with a bill.{/trap} {reward}The pleasures of Paradise come with none.{/reward}
old: Every pleasure has a price I pay later.
new: Allah can give joy with nothing taken from me in return.
try: Skip one pleasure today that you know leaves you feeling worse afterward.

title: They pick whatever fruit they like.
subtitle: Choosing is part of the reward
then: Ibn Kathir says {reward}whatever fruits they wish for{/reward} will be handed around among them. For listeners in a dry valley where fruit was scarce, the picture was of plenty and of choice.
now: The supermarket shelf where you check the price before you check what you want. The menu you read from right to left. {reward}There, you pick by what you love, not by what you can afford.{/reward}
old: My wants will always be limited by my budget.
new: Allah delights in giving His people the very thing they would choose.
try: Share a piece of fruit with someone today and thank Allah for it before the first bite.

title: Whatever they crave is already prepared.
subtitle: Desire met, not just need
then: After fruit comes {reward}the flesh of birds, from whatever they desire{/reward}. Ibn Kathir explains the two verses together: fruit they choose, meat they wish for. Paradise meets not only need but appetite.
now: You eat lunch at your desk, the same sandwich every day, because it is fast. You forget what you even like. {reward}The verse speaks to the you who has a real appetite{/reward}, not the one rushing through.
old: Wanting nice things is a little shameful.
new: Allah Himself names my desires as something He will honor there.
try: Cook or share a meal someone you love enjoys, and eat it slowly together.

title: Companions with beautiful wide eyes await them.
subtitle: Companionship is part of the reward
then: The list of gifts moves from food to {reward}companions with wide, lovely eyes{/reward}. The verse names it briefly and with dignity. For people who knew loss and lonely nights, companionship was a gift worth naming.
now: Married or not, you know the empty room at the end of a hard day, the message you wish someone would send. {reward}Paradise answers loneliness too{/reward}, purely and without hurt.
old: Loneliness is just something I have to carry forever.
new: Allah included companionship in His promise, so my longing is seen.
try: Message one person today who might feel alone, just to ask how they are.

title: Like pearls kept safe in their shells.
subtitle: Beauty that was protected and unspoiled
then: The verse compares them to {reward}pearls well protected{/reward}. A pearl kept in its shell is never scratched, dulled, or passed from hand to hand. The image is of beauty that was guarded and stayed pure.
now: You keep your phone in a case so the screen won't crack. You guard the things that matter. {idea}What Allah treasures, He keeps protected.{/idea} That includes the heart you guard from what spoils it.
old: Holding back and guarding myself makes me miss out.
new: What is protected keeps its shine.
try: Guard one thing today: your eyes from one scroll, or your tongue from one remark.

title: All of it is a reward for what they did.
subtitle: The gifts are tied to deeds
then: After the list of thrones, cups, fruit and companions, one line explains it: {idea}a reward for what they used to do{/idea}. The words used to do point to habits kept over a lifetime, not a single act.
now: Your morning is mostly autopilot: alarm, phone, coffee, commute. {idea}What you used to do{/idea} is what you keep doing on a normal Tuesday. That is what gets rewarded.
old: One big good deed someday will make up for my ordinary days.
new: My ordinary, repeated habits are what my reward is built from.
try: Pick one tiny good habit, two minutes long, and do it at the same time today and tomorrow.

title: No gossip, no insults, no empty talk there.
subtitle: The sound of Paradise is clean
then: Among the gifts is something absent: {reward}they hear no vain talk and no sinful speech{/reward}. It is listed with the thrones and the cups, as a gift in itself: a place without a single harmful word.
now: The comment section under any post. The office kitchen when someone leaves the room. The family chat after a wedding. {trap}So much of what you hear wears you down.{/trap} The verse promises quiet from all of it.
old: Gossip is just background noise; it doesn't really affect me.
new: Paradise is free of it, which tells me how much it harms me here.
try: Leave or mute one conversation today that is turning into gossip.

title: Only one word fills the air: peace, peace.
subtitle: What they do hear
then: After saying what is absent, the verse says what is present: {reward}only the saying, Peace, peace{/reward}. The greeting goes out and comes back, again and again. With this, the description of the foremost's reward is complete.
now: You walk into the house after work. Someone looks up from the sofa, says salam, and means it. The tension drops. {reward}Imagine every word you hear being that.{/reward}
old: Saying salam is just a habit, a word at the door.
new: Salam is the language of Paradise, practiced here.
try: Say salam fully and warmly to everyone in your home today, and wait for the reply.

title: Now the people of the right: how fortunate they are!
subtitle: The second group, the righteous believers
then: After the foremost, the surah turns to {reward}those on the right, the righteous believers{/reward}. Maymun bin Mihran said they are lesser in rank than the foremost. The verse asks about them, then answers with a full picture of their home.
now: You are not the one who memorized the whole Quran or fasts every Monday. You pray, you try, you slip, you come back. {reward}This verse is about people like you{/reward}, and it calls them fortunate.
old: If I'm not one of the very best, Paradise isn't really for me.
new: The right is a real, honored place for ordinary striving believers.
try: Write down three good things you do regularly, and thank Allah for each one.

title: The lote tree, with its thorns removed.
subtitle: A familiar tree, made perfect
then: Many scholars said Sidr Makhdud is {reward}the kind without thorns{/reward}, and Ibn Abbas said it is laden with fruit. Ibn Kathir notes the lote tree of this life is thorny with little fruit; in Paradise it is the opposite. Mujahid said the Quraysh loved its shade.
now: Every good thing here has its thorn: the job with the long commute, the family you love who can also hurt you. {reward}A tree with the thorns taken out{/reward} is good without the sting.
old: Every blessing comes with a catch.
new: Allah can give me the fruit with the thorns removed.
try: Name one thorn in a blessing you have, and thank Allah for the blessing anyway.

title: Trees heavy with fruit, layer upon layer.
subtitle: Abundance stacked on abundance

row.title: talh
sub: a thorny shrub of the Hijaz

then: Talh was a large thorny shrub in the Hijaz whose shade the Quraysh liked. Mujahid said {reward}its fruits are piled on top of each other{/reward}. Many, including Ibn Abbas and Abu Hurayrah, said it means the banana tree.
now: You know a market stall piled with bananas, bunch over bunch, more than anyone could carry home. {reward}That kind of plenty{/reward} is the picture, drawn from a tree the listeners already knew.
old: Good things are always scarce and rationed.
new: Allah describes Paradise with plenty piled on plenty.
try: Share some of your food today with someone, so your table has a little of that plenty.

title: Shade that stretches farther than you can ride.
subtitle: A shade a rider crosses for a hundred years
then: The Prophet ﷺ said, as Al-Bukhari and Muslim recorded, that in Paradise is {reward}a tree whose shade a rider can travel for a hundred years without passing it{/reward}, and then recited this verse. To desert travelers, shade meant life.
now: The car parked in the sun all day, the bus stop with no roof, the summer walk home. You hunt for any patch of shade. {reward}This shade never ends.{/reward}
old: Relief in life always runs out quickly.
new: Allah's relief can be wider than any distance I could travel.
try: Next time you step into shade on a hot day, ask Allah for the extended shade.

title: Water that keeps on pouring.
subtitle: Constant water for a thirsty people
then: To the trees and the shade, the verse adds {reward}water flowing constantly{/reward}. For people living in a dry valley, running water that no one had to draw or carry was a picture of wealth and rest.
now: The water bill you check, the tap that sputters, the bottle you carry to the gym and ration. {reward}Water that keeps pouring{/reward} is ease without counting.
old: I take water for granted until it stops.
new: Water is a gift here and a promise there.
try: Make wudu slowly today and notice the water as a blessing.

title: Fruit in plenty, of every kind.
subtitle: Looks familiar, tastes new

row.title: looks familiar
sub: this is what we had before

then: Ibn Kathir says they will have {reward}plenty of fruits of various kinds{/reward}, and links it to the verse where the people of Paradise say this is what we were given before. The shape will look similar, but the taste is different.
now: You bite into the first mango of the season and it tastes better than you remembered. {reward}Paradise is that surprise, every time{/reward}, something familiar becoming new.
old: I've tasted everything this life has to offer.
new: Allah has joys waiting that only look familiar.
try: Eat one fruit slowly today and name one thing you love about its taste.

title: Never out of season, never out of reach.
subtitle: No end to the supply, no barrier to taking it
then: Ibn Kathir explains that {reward}the supply never runs out, winter or summer{/reward}, and nothing keeps them from reaching it. Two limits we know well, scarcity and barriers, are both removed.
now: Your favorite fruit is out of season, or it is there but too expensive this week, or it sits on a high shelf behind glass. {reward}Neither limit exists there.{/reward}
old: There is always something standing between me and what I want.
new: In Paradise, nothing stands between the believer and the good.
try: Remove one barrier for someone today: pay for a coffee, carry a bag, lend a charger.

title: Their beds are raised high.
subtitle: Comfort and honor together
then: The list of gifts for those on the right reaches their resting place: {reward}couches raised high{/reward}. A raised couch speaks of both comfort and honor, rest given to a welcome guest.
now: The thin mattress, the night shift, the sofa you fall asleep on with the TV still on. You rarely rest well. {reward}A raised bed of honor{/reward} is rest as a gift, not a collapse.
old: Rest is just what I grab when I'm too tired to go on.
new: Real rest is a gift Allah promises to those who strive.
try: Tonight, make wudu and say the bedtime dua before you lie down.

title: Allah creates them anew.
subtitle: A new creation, free of old wear and tear
then: Allah says {reward}We have produced them in a new creation{/reward}, with Himself as the One acting. After trees, water and couches, the verses turn to the people of Paradise themselves, made fresh.
now: You look in the mirror after a hard year: gray hairs, tired eyes, a back that aches in the morning. {idea}Age and wear are real here.{/idea} {reward}The verse promises a creation that is new.{/reward}
old: My body only goes one way: older and more tired.
new: Allah, who created me once, can create me anew.
try: Next time you notice a sign of age in yourself, say: O Allah, make what is coming better than what has passed.

title: Made pure and untouched.
subtitle: Freshness given as a gift
then: The description continues: Allah {reward}made them virgins{/reward}. The Quran states it briefly, as a gift of purity and freshness, and moves on. Allah is again the One who does the making.
now: So much around you is secondhand: the used car, the hand-me-down coat, a heart bruised by old hurts. {reward}The verse speaks of something given fresh{/reward}, never used up.
old: Nothing stays fresh; everything gets used up.
new: Allah can give something entirely fresh, untouched by any past hurt.
try: Ask Allah today to heal one old hurt in your heart and make it new.

title: Loving to their husbands, and of matching age.
subtitle: Love that fits, with no gap and no distance
then: The verse gives two qualities: {reward}devoted to their husbands, and of equal age{/reward}. It completes the picture of companionship among those on the right: love that is returned, and partners well matched.
now: A couple sits side by side on the sofa, each on a phone. Small distances grow quietly. {reward}The verse describes love without distance{/reward}, and you can start practicing it now.
old: Closeness in marriage fades, and that's just normal.
new: Warm, devoted love is part of what Allah calls reward.
try: Put your phone away for ten minutes tonight and give your full attention to someone you love.

title: All of this is for the people of the right.
subtitle: The list ends with whom it belongs to

row.title: for the right
sub: those who believed and did good

then: After the trees, shade, water, fruit and companions, the verse says plainly whom it is for: {reward}the companions of the right{/reward}. Not only the foremost, but the righteous believers just below them in rank.
now: You scroll past people who seem holier than you and think Paradise belongs to them. {reward}This verse addresses the gift to the right{/reward}, a crowd that ordinary believers can join.
old: This sounds wonderful, but it's for people better than me.
new: It is named for the people of the right, and I can be among them.
try: Do one ordinary good deed today with the intention of being among the people of the right.

title: A large company from the earlier ones.
subtitle: Many from the early generations are on the right
then: Earlier, the foremost were a crowd from the earlier ones and {trap}only a few from the later{/trap}. Here the people of the right are {reward}a large company from the earlier ones{/reward}, and the next verse balances it.
now: Your grandparents' generation prayed through hard times without apps, podcasts or lectures on demand. {reward}Many like them are in this company.{/reward} The verse honors those who came before you.
old: Older generations had simpler faith; it doesn't compare.
new: Many before me are among the right, and I can join their company.
try: Make dua today for your grandparents and the believers who came before them.

title: And a large company from the later ones too.
subtitle: The good news the Companions had hoped for
then: Abu Hurayrah reported that when the verses said {trap}only a few from the later ones{/trap}, it was hard for the Companions. Then these verses came, and the Prophet ﷺ said he hoped his Ummah would be {reward}half the people of Paradise{/reward}.
now: Sometimes you think the real believers lived long ago and you were born too late. {reward}This verse is about you, too.{/reward} A large company of the later ones means the door is wide.
old: I was born too late for the best of faith.
new: Allah promised a large company from the later ones, and that includes my generation.
try: Tell a friend one hopeful thing about faith today instead of a complaint about our times.

title: And the people of the left: how wretched they are!
subtitle: The third group, described plainly
then: After the right, the surah turns to {trap}those on the left{/trap}, with the same form of question. Ibn Kathir says it means: what is their condition? The answer follows over the next verses.
now: A doctor shows you a scan and says: this is where your habits lead if nothing changes. It is hard to hear. {idea}The warning comes before, not after.{/idea}
old: Hearing about the left side just makes me anxious.
new: The warning is a mercy that comes while I can still turn.
try: Say astaghfirullah ten times today, slowly, thinking of one thing you know you need to change.

title: A scorching wind and boiling water.
subtitle: The reverse of shade and flowing water
then: Ibn Kathir explains Samum as {trap}a fierce hot wind{/trap} and Hamim as boiling water. Those on the right were given extended shade and flowing water. The left is given the reverse of both.
now: On a summer day you know the difference between a cool breeze and the blast from a car exhaust. {idea}The verse uses what you already feel{/idea} to make the warning real, so you choose the shade.
old: Comfort and discomfort just happen to me.
new: The ease I hope for on that Day is built from choices I make here.
try: When you feel the heat today, ask Allah to protect you from the heat of the Fire.

title: Their only shade is black smoke.
subtitle: Shade that gives no relief
then: Ibn Abbas and others said Yahmum is {trap}the shadow of black smoke{/trap}. Ibn Kathir links it to another verse about a shadow in three columns that gives no shade and is of no use against the flame.
now: Some things look like relief: the scroll at 1 a.m., the drink to forget, the revenge text. {trap}Shade made of smoke.{/trap} It looks like rest and leaves you worse.
old: Anything that takes my mind off things is relief.
new: Some relief is smoke: it looks like shade and gives none.
try: Name one false comfort you reach for when stressed, and swap it once today for wudu, a walk, or a call.

title: Neither cool nor kind.
subtitle: No breeze, no beauty, no benefit
then: The smoke shade is {trap}neither cool nor Karim{/trap}. Ibn Kathir says it brings no soft breeze, and Al-Hasan and Qatadah said its sight is not pleasant. It has the shape of shade with none of the gift.
now: The job you took for the money that gives you nothing else. The friendship that only drains you. {idea}Something can have the shape of good and be empty inside.{/idea}
old: If it looks like what I wanted, it must be good for me.
new: I should test what I chase by whether it actually cools and benefits.
try: Look at one thing you rely on and ask honestly: does this actually do me good?

title: Before that, they were lost in luxury.
subtitle: Comfort that made them deaf
then: Allah gives the reason: {trap}before that, they indulged in luxury{/trap}. Ibn Kathir says they enjoyed life's pleasures and satisfied their desires, all while ignoring what the Messengers brought them.
now: Payday, a new phone, a weekend away, another parcel at the door. Nothing wrong with any of it, until {trap}you are too busy enjoying to listen{/trap}. The danger is comfort that makes you deaf.
old: As long as I'm enjoying life, I'm doing fine.
new: Comfort is a test of whether I still listen to Allah.
try: Before your next purchase or treat, say bismillah, and alhamdulillah after.

title: They kept at the great sin and never turned back.
subtitle: Persisting, not slipping, was the problem
then: Ibn Kathir says they {trap}persisted and did not intend to repent{/trap}. Ibn Abbas and others said the great sin is idolatry, claiming rivals as gods besides Allah. The weight of the verse falls on persisting.
now: You slip, you feel bad, you come back. That is human. {trap}The danger is deciding you won't even try anymore.{/trap} {idea}The door of turning back stays open while you breathe.{/idea}
old: I've done this so many times; it's too late to stop.
new: What ruins a person is refusing to turn back, not falling.
try: Pick one sin you keep repeating. Today, sincerely intend to leave it and ask Allah for help.

title: They mocked: once we are dust and bones, back again?
subtitle: Their denial, in their own words
then: Those on the left {trap}used to say: when we die and become dust and bones, shall we be raised?{/trap} Ibn Kathir says they said it denying and rejecting the resurrection. The surah introduction names this as the core doubt in Makkah.
now: You stand at a graveside and a thought creeps in: this is it, then nothing. {trap}It sounds like realism.{/trap} {idea}The surah answers with how you were made the first time.{/idea}
old: Once someone is buried and gone, it really is over.
new: The One who made me from nothing can make me again.
try: Visit or remember a grave today and say: to Allah we belong and to Him we return.

title: Even our forefathers, long gone?
subtitle: Mocking the return of old generations
then: They added: {trap}and our forefathers too?{/trap} Ancestors dead for generations seemed even further from coming back. Ibn Kathir says they said it in denial and rejection.
now: You look at a faded photo of your great-grandparents, names half-forgotten. It is hard to picture them standing again. {idea}For Allah, the time in between is nothing.{/idea}
old: People gone that long are just history.
new: Every generation, mine and theirs, is waiting for the same Day.
try: Make dua for your forefathers by name, as far back as you know them.

title: Tell them: the first and the last, all of them.
subtitle: The Prophet ﷺ is told how to answer
then: Allah tells the Prophet ﷺ: {idea}say, the earlier and the later generations{/idea}. Ibn Kathir says all the Children of Adam will be gathered for the Day and none of them will be left out. The answer to and our forefathers? is yes, and you.
now: In a crowd at the airport or a stadium, you feel invisible, one of thousands. {idea}On the Day, no one is lost in the crowd.{/idea} Each person is called.
old: Among billions of people, my life is too small to matter.
new: Not one person is skipped, so my life fully counts.
try: Today, do one deed as if it will be shown to you personally, because it will.

title: Gathered for a Day already fixed.
subtitle: Not early, not late, not a minute off
then: All will be gathered {idea}for the appointment of a known Day{/idea}. Ibn Kathir says that time is precisely set. It will not come late or early, nor increase or decrease.
now: Your flight has a departure time printed on the ticket. You plan your whole day around it. {idea}This appointment is fixed too{/idea}, though you never see the ticket.
old: Since I don't know the date, I don't need to plan for it.
new: Not knowing the date is a reason to be ready every day.
try: Settle one thing today you would want settled before that appointment: a debt, an apology.

title: Then you who strayed and denied...
subtitle: The warning turns direct
then: The verse now speaks to them directly: {trap}then indeed you, the erring ones, the deniers{/trap}. It names two qualities together. They strayed from the way, and they denied the truth when it came.
now: Drifting starts small: one missed prayer, then a week of them. Then one day you hear a reminder and roll your eyes. {trap}Straying has turned into denying.{/trap} {idea}Catch the drift early.{/idea}
old: Drifting a bit from faith is harmless; I'll come back.
new: Straying left alone can harden into denial, so I return early.
try: If you have drifted from one practice, do it once today, however small.

title: Their food will be from the tree of Zaqqum.
subtitle: A meal no one would choose
then: Ibn Kathir says they {trap}will be seized and made to eat from the Zaqqum tree{/trap}. The contrast with the right is sharp: there, fruit they choose and meat they desire. Here, food no one would pick.
now: You eat what is in front of you without thinking about how you paid for it or whom you stepped over to get it. {idea}What you take in here is part of what you will answer for there.{/idea}
old: What I consume is my private business.
new: Everything I take in, I will one day account for.
try: Before eating today, think for a moment about whether the way you earned it pleases Allah.

title: And they fill their bellies with it.
subtitle: Full, and still no relief
then: They will eat {trap}until their stomachs become full{/trap}, Ibn Kathir says. Being full is usually a comfort. Here it is only more of what harms.
now: You eat until you are stuffed and still feel empty. You buy more and still want. {trap}Full is not the same as satisfied.{/trap} {idea}Only what Allah gives truly satisfies.{/idea}
old: If I get enough, I'll finally feel satisfied.
new: More of the wrong thing never satisfies.
try: Stop eating one meal today a little before you are full, and say alhamdulillah.

title: Then boiling water on top of it.
subtitle: No drink to bring relief
then: After the Zaqqum comes {trap}Hamim, boiling water{/trap}. Where a person expects a drink to bring relief, there is none. The people of the right drank from a flowing spring.
now: You grab an energy drink to fix the tiredness from a late night, and the late night repeats. {trap}The fix becomes part of the problem.{/trap} {idea}Break the loop while you can.{/idea}
old: I can fix one harm by adding another.
new: Relief from the wrong source only adds harm.
try: Notice one fix you use that feeds the problem. Swap it once today.

title: Drinking like camels with a thirst that never ends.
subtitle: Thirst that is never quenched
then: Ibn Abbas and others said Al-Him are thirsty camels. As-Suddi said it is {trap}a disease that makes camels drink and never be satisfied{/trap}. The people of Hell will never quench their thirst.
now: Some cravings work like that: the more likes, the more you need; the more you buy, the more you want. {trap}A thirst that drinking only deepens.{/trap} {idea}Ask Allah for a content heart.{/idea}
old: If I just get more, the craving will stop.
new: Some thirsts grow by being fed, so I should stop feeding them.
try: Say this dua today: O Allah, make me content with what You have given me.

title: That is the welcome they get on the Day of Recompense.
subtitle: A guest's welcome, reversed
then: The word is nuzul, the hospitality offered to a guest. Ibn Kathir says {trap}this is their entertainment with their Lord on the Day of Reckoning{/trap}, and contrasts it with the believers, for whom the Gardens of Firdaws are a welcome of honor.
now: You arrive at a relative's house after a long trip. The way they receive you says what they think of you. {idea}Everyone arrives as a guest that Day.{/idea} What welcome are you preparing for?
old: I'll worry about how I'm received when I get there.
new: The welcome I get then is what I prepare now.
try: Host someone kindly today, even with just tea, and ask Allah for the welcome of the believers.

title: We created you. So why not believe?
subtitle: Your first life is the proof of the second
then: The deniers asked: when we become dust and bones, shall we be raised? Allah replies: {idea}We created you{/idea}. Ibn Kathir explains: He created you after you were nothing, so is not the One who began creation more able to bring it back?
now: You look at your own baby photo, or at your child asleep. A few years earlier that person did not exist. {idea}You already happened once, from nothing.{/idea} The second time is not harder.
old: Life after death is hard to believe.
new: My own existence is the evidence that it is possible.
try: Look at your hand for a moment today and say: You made this from nothing.

title: Look at the drop you came from.
subtitle: A question meant to make you think
then: Allah asks the listeners to {idea}look at the semen they emit{/idea}. Ibn Kathir explains the question: is it you who makes it settle in the womb and creates life from it, stage after stage? The argument is made personal.
now: The first scan: a tiny flicker on a screen in a dim clinic room, and your heart racing. {idea}No one in that room built that heartbeat.{/idea}
old: Making a baby is just a natural process.
new: Every new life is Allah creating, and I am one of them.
try: Congratulate someone who recently had a baby, or make dua for a couple hoping for one.

title: Is it you who creates it, or is it Us?
subtitle: Taking credit versus giving it
then: The question is direct: {idea}is it you who creates it, or are We the Creator?{/idea} Ibn Kathir's answer is that Allah is the One who does all of it. Parents are the means, not the makers.
now: Parents post the newborn photo with a proud caption. The pride is natural. {trap}But no parent designed a single cell.{/trap} {idea}Gratitude is the honest caption.{/idea}
old: My children, my body, my health are my own work.
new: I am the means. Allah is the Creator.
try: Next time you feel proud of something you have, add quietly: this is from Allah.

title: Death is decreed for all, and Allah is never outrun.
subtitle: Death is equal, and His power is total
then: Allah says {idea}We have decreed death among you{/idea}. Ad-Dahhak said Allah made everyone in the heavens and the earth equal with regard to death. We are not outstripped, Ibn Kathir explains, means He is never unable.
now: Rich or poor, gym or no gym, the hospital corridor holds everyone the same way. {idea}Death is the one equal thing.{/idea} Looking after your health is good, but no one outruns the appointment.
old: With enough care and money, I can stay ahead of death.
new: Death is decreed equally, so I prepare instead of running.
try: Spend five minutes today thinking about one thing you would want to finish before you die.

title: He can remake you in forms you do not know.
subtitle: Resurrection is not limited by our imagination
then: Allah is never unable {idea}to change your shapes on the Day of Resurrection{/idea}, Ibn Kathir explains, and create you in forms you do not know. The listeners could not picture a resurrection. The verse says that is no limit for Allah.
now: Twenty years ago you could not have pictured the phone in your pocket. {trap}What you can't picture is not the edge of what is possible.{/trap} Allah's power is not measured by your imagination.
old: If I can't imagine how resurrection works, it's hard to believe.
new: My imagination is not the limit of Allah's power.
try: When something about faith is hard to picture today, say: Allah is able, and leave it there.

title: You know the first creation. Why not reflect?
subtitle: The memory that answers the doubt
then: Ibn Kathir explains: {idea}you know that Allah created you after you were nothing{/idea}, and gave you hearing, sight and hearts. Will you not remember that the One who made you first is more able to bring you back?
now: You ask for signs while ignoring your own heartbeat, the eyes reading this line, the breath in your chest. {idea}The proof isn't missing. Attention is.{/idea}
old: I'd believe more strongly if I had more evidence.
new: The evidence is my own life. I need to remember it.
try: Take three slow breaths today and remember with each one that you were made.

title: Look at the seeds you plant.
subtitle: Your effort and His growing
then: Allah turns to farming: {idea}do you see what you sow?{/idea} Ibn Kathir explains it as tilling the earth and planting seeds. Abu Hurayrah reported that the Prophet ﷺ taught people to say I tilled, rather than I made it grow.
now: You plant tomatoes on the balcony, start a small business, raise a child. You do the work: watering, planning, waking up early. {idea}You sow.{/idea} The growing is not in your hands.
old: My results come from my effort.
new: My effort is sowing. The growing comes from Allah.
try: Before starting one task today, say: I sow, You make it grow.

title: Is it you who makes it grow, or Us?
subtitle: Credit where it belongs
then: Allah asks: {idea}is it you that make it grow, or are We the Grower?{/idea} Ibn Kathir says Allah causes the seeds to stay firm and grow inside the earth, out of His compassion and mercy.
now: A promotion, good exam grades, a deal that finally closes. It feels like your skill did it. {idea}Skill is the seed. Growth is a mercy.{/idea}
old: My success is proof of my talent.
new: My success is Allah's mercy working through my effort.
try: Thank Allah out loud for one recent success, naming it.

title: He could turn it to dry stubble overnight.
subtitle: The harvest is never guaranteed
then: Ibn Kathir explains: {trap}if Allah wills, He could dry the crops before they ripen{/trap}. Tafakkahun means you would be left wondering, blaming each other, or grieving, as Ikrimah, Al-Hasan and Qatadah said.
now: The project you worked on for months gets cancelled the week before launch. You stare at the screen, blaming yourself, then everyone else. {idea}Every harvest that does arrive is a gift.{/idea}
old: If I do everything right, the result is guaranteed.
new: Every harvest that reaches me is mercy, not a given.
try: Think of one thing that went right this week and thank Allah that it did not fall apart.

title: We are ruined, they would cry.
subtitle: The first reaction to loss
then: Allah describes what they would say: {trap}we are indeed Mughramun{/trap}. Ibn Kathir explains it as ruined. Mujahid and Ikrimah said it means being the target of revenge, and Qatadah said they would sometimes cry, we were punished.
now: The car breaks down in the same week the rent is due. Your first words: I'm finished. {trap}Panic speaks first.{/trap} The verse shows you that reaction so you can catch it in yourself.
old: When things fall apart, I'm ruined.
new: Loss is real, but the One who grew it can give again.
try: When something goes wrong today, say inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi rajiun before anything else.

title: No, we have been deprived.
subtitle: From feeling ruined to feeling robbed
then: Then they would say: {trap}nay, we are deprived{/trap}. Qatadah said they would say we were punished at some times and we were deprived at others. The feeling moves from loss to grievance, as if something owed had been taken.
now: Someone else gets the promotion you were counting on. You feel robbed. {trap}But it was never yours yet.{/trap} {idea}Provision is given, not owed.{/idea}
old: When I lose what I expected, I've been cheated.
new: Everything I receive is a gift, so losing it is not theft.
try: Think of one thing you feel robbed of and say: it was Yours to give, O Allah.

title: Look at the water you drink.
subtitle: The most ordinary miracle
then: After the crops, Allah points to something even closer: {idea}the water that you drink{/idea}. The same question returns: look at it, and ask who brings it to you.
now: You fill a bottle at the office cooler without thinking. Half the time you leave it unfinished on the desk. {idea}The verse asks you to really look at it, once.{/idea}
old: Water is just there; it's nothing special.
new: Every drink of water is sent to me by Allah.
try: Drink your next glass of water sitting down, with bismillah before and alhamdulillah after.

title: Did you bring it down from the clouds?
subtitle: Rain is in no one's control but His
then: Allah asks: {idea}is it you who brought it down from the clouds, or We?{/idea} Ibn Abbas and Mujahid said Al-Muzn means the clouds. Ibn Kathir says Allah is the One who causes the rain to fall.
now: The weather app says 80 percent chance of rain and you plan around it. In a drought, everyone checks the same app with worry. {idea}No app sends rain.{/idea}
old: Weather is just a system that runs itself.
new: Rain is sent, and the Sender can be thanked.
try: Next time it rains, go to the window and make a dua.

title: He could make it salty. So why no thanks?
subtitle: Fresh water is a choice He makes for you
then: Ibn Kathir explains that Allah could make the rain {trap}salty, sour, undrinkable and unfit for plants{/trap}. Then He asks: {idea}why do you not give thanks?{/idea} He links it to the verse about rain that grows crops, olives, dates and grapes.
now: You only notice water when the tap runs brown or the bill doubles. {idea}Gratitude usually waits for loss.{/idea} The verse asks you to thank before that.
old: I'll be grateful when something special happens.
new: Every sip of fresh water is reason enough to thank Allah.
try: Say alhamdulillah after every drink of water today.

title: Look at the fire you light.
subtitle: The flame you strike every day
then: The third sign is fire: {idea}do you see the fire which you kindle?{/idea} Ibn Kathir says the Arabs rubbed green branches of two trees, Al-Markh and Al-Afar, against each other, and sparks would fly out.
now: You click the stove on for tea, flick a lighter, turn up the heater. {idea}Fire is so normal you never look at it.{/idea} The verse asks you to look.
old: Fire is just a utility I switch on.
new: Even the flame on my stove is a sign from Allah.
try: When you light the stove today, say bismillah and watch the flame for one second.

title: Did you make the tree that feeds the flame?
subtitle: Even the fuel was created
then: Allah asks: {idea}is it you who produced its tree, or are We the Producer?{/idea} Ibn Kathir says Allah is the One who made kindling fire possible. The branches that sparked were from trees He grew.
now: Gas in the pipes, wood in the stove, fuel at the station. {idea}You strike the spark, but every fuel was grown or stored by Allah{/idea} long before you were born.
old: I produce what I use.
new: I only use what Allah produced.
try: Switch off one light or heater you don't need today, as thanks for the energy Allah gave.

title: Fire is a reminder and a provision for travelers.
subtitle: Comfort here, and a warning about there
then: Mujahid and Qatadah said fire is {idea}a reminder of the Hellfire{/idea}; the Prophet ﷺ said this fire is one part of seventy of the Fire of Hell. It is also {reward}a provision{/reward}: Ibn Abbas said for travelers, Mujahid said for everyone who cooks and needs warmth.
now: On a cold camping night the fire is everything: warmth, food, light, faces glowing around it. {idea}The same flame that comforts you also reminds you.{/idea}
old: Fire is just warmth and cooking.
new: Every flame is both a gift and a gentle warning.
try: When you feel the warmth of a heater or stove today, ask Allah to protect you from the Fire.

title: So glorify the name of your Lord, the Most Great.
subtitle: The right response to seed, water and fire
then: After creation, crops, rain and fire, the passage ends with a command: {reward}glorify the name of your Lord, the Most Great{/reward}. The signs are not a science lesson. They lead to praise.
now: You finish your tea, wipe the counter, scroll to the next thing. {idea}Seed, water, fire: you used all three before breakfast.{/idea} The verse asks for one sentence of praise.
old: Noticing blessings is enough.
new: Noticing blessings should end in praising the One who gave them.
try: After your next meal, say subhana Rabbiyal Azim three times.

title: No! I swear by the places where the stars set.
subtitle: An oath before a claim about the Quran
then: Ibn Kathir says the No that opens the oath rejects their claim: {trap}the matter is not as you say, that the Quran is magic or sorcery{/trap}. Mujahid said the stars' Mawaqi are their positions of rising and setting. The oath is made by something vast and orderly.
now: On a clear night away from the city lights, you look up and the stars move in perfect order. {idea}Allah swears by that order{/idea} before telling you what His Book is.
old: The Quran is one more book among many.
new: The One who orders the stars stands behind this Book.
try: Look at the night sky tonight for one minute, then read a few verses of the Quran.

title: It is a mighty oath, if only you knew.
subtitle: The size of the oath shows the size of the truth
then: Ibn Kathir explains: {idea}if you knew the greatness of this oath, you would know the greatness of what it is sworn about{/idea}. It is Allah who is making the oath, and the oath tells you how much is at stake.
now: When someone says I swear on my mother's life, you know how serious they are. {idea}Allah swears by the positions of the stars.{/idea} Think how serious the next sentence must be.
old: Oaths in the Quran are just a style of speaking.
new: The bigger the oath, the more closely I should listen.
try: Read the next verses of this surah slowly today, as if hearing them under oath.

title: Truly, this is a noble Quran.
subtitle: What the great oath was sworn for
then: The oath lands: {reward}this is indeed an honorable recitation{/reward}. Ibn Kathir says this Quran, revealed to Muhammad ﷺ, is a glorious Book. It answers the Makkan suspicion that it was magic or sorcery.
now: The Quran app on your phone sits between a chat app and a game. {idea}It is easy to give it the same weight as everything else on the screen.{/idea} This verse calls it noble.
old: Reading Quran is one more task on my list.
new: Reading Quran is time spent with something noble.
try: Open the Quran today before you open any other app.

title: Kept in a well-guarded Book.
subtitle: Protected before it ever reached us
then: The Quran is {idea}in a Book Maknun{/idea}, which Ibn Kathir explains as glorious, well guarded and revered. Ibn Abbas said it is the Book that is in heaven. Its source is protected.
now: Your important files live in the cloud with backups and a password, and you trust they are safe. {idea}The Quran's source is guarded far beyond that.{/idea}
old: Who knows how this text really came to be?
new: This Book was guarded at its source by Allah.
try: Hold a printed mushaf today, or open one, and remember where it comes from.

title: None touch it but the purified.
subtitle: The pure angels carry it, not devils
then: Ibn Abbas and many others said {reward}the pure ones are the angels{/reward}. Ibn Zayd said the Quraysh claimed devils brought the Quran down, and Allah answered that only the pure touch it. The surah introduction tells how Umar's sister quoted this verse when he asked to read the pages.
now: Before opening the Quran, you wash your hands, maybe make wudu, and find somewhere quiet. {idea}Your small preparation echoes the purity of those who carry it.{/idea}
old: It doesn't matter how I come to the Quran.
new: The Quran is carried by the pure, so I come to it with care.
try: Make wudu before you read Quran today, and notice how it changes your focus.

title: Sent down from the Lord of all the worlds.
subtitle: Not magic, not poetry, but revelation

row.title: revelation
sub: the truth, no doubt in it

then: Ibn Kathir says {idea}this Quran is a revelation from the Lord of all that exists{/idea}, not magic, sorcery or poetry as they said. It is the truth, with no doubt in it.
now: You read advice threads, self-help books, a podcast host's opinions. Helpful, mixed, human. {idea}This one is from the Lord of the worlds.{/idea}
old: The Quran is good advice, like other good books.
new: The Quran is revelation from the One who made everything.
try: Read one verse today and ask: what is my Lord telling me here?

title: Is this the message you treat so lightly?
subtitle: Brushing it off is a response too
then: Allah asks: {trap}is it such a talk that you are Mudhinun?{/trap} Ibn Abbas said it means you do not believe in it and you deny it. Mujahid said it means relying on something other than it. Either way, a noble message is met with a shrug.
now: A reminder comes up on your feed: a verse, a short talk. {trap}You scroll past, not against it, just not interested.{/trap} {idea}Indifference is still a response.{/idea}
old: I'm not rejecting the Quran, I'm just busy.
new: Treating it lightly is a response too, and I can choose better.
try: The next time a verse or reminder appears in front of you today, stop and read it fully.

title: Is your thanks for provision to deny the Provider?
subtitle: Rain comes, and the credit goes to a star
then: Ibn Abbas read it as {trap}you make your thanks that you deny{/trap}, saying that whenever it rained, some would credit a star. After a rainy night at Al-Hudaybiyah, the Prophet ﷺ said that whoever says {reward}we were given rain by Allah's blessing and mercy{/reward} believes in Him.
now: Your salary arrives and you credit your boss, the economy, your hustle. {trap}Everything gets the credit except Allah.{/trap} The verse asks where your thanks actually goes.
old: Good things come from the right conditions and my smart choices.
new: The conditions are tools. The provision is from Allah.
try: When your next payment or piece of good news arrives, say first: this is by the blessing of Allah.

title: Then why, when the soul reaches the throat...
subtitle: The moment no one can argue with
then: Ibn Kathir explains Al-Hulqum as {trap}the throat, at the time of death{/trap}. He links it to another verse where the soul reaches the collarbone and people ask who can cure him. The surah now places the reader beside a deathbed.
now: The hospital corridor, the machines beeping, family speaking in whispers. Everyone wants to do something and no one can. {idea}That helplessness is the argument.{/idea}
old: With enough medicine and money, death can usually be held off.
new: When the time comes, no one can hold the soul back.
try: Visit or call someone who is sick today.

title: And you are looking on, helpless.
subtitle: Watching, but powerless
then: Ibn Kathir says {idea}you are looking at the dying person, witnessing the stupor of death{/idea}. The verse reminds the listeners of what many of them had already seen with their own eyes.
now: You hold your grandmother's hand in a ward at 3 a.m. The nurse is kind and the doctors have tried. {idea}You are looking on.{/idea} All that is left is to pray.
old: I'll handle death when it comes to my family.
new: At death I can only watch, so I prepare my heart now.
try: Make dua today, by name, for someone you love who is ill or elderly.

title: We are nearer to him than you, but you do not see.
subtitle: The angels are already in the room
then: Allah says {idea}We are nearer to him than you{/idea}. Ibn Kathir explains: with Our angels, whom you cannot see. He links it to the verse about the messengers who take the soul and never neglect their duty.
now: The room feels full: family, nurses, the hum of the monitor. {idea}It is fuller than you know.{/idea} At that moment, the unseen is the closest thing in the room.
old: What I can see is all that's happening.
new: At the most important moments, the unseen is nearest.
try: Sit quietly for one minute today and remember that Allah's knowledge is nearer to you than anyone.

title: If you will never be judged, then why not...
subtitle: A challenge to those who deny the reckoning

row.title: we are owned
sub: we cannot even keep our souls

then: Sa'id bin Jubayr and Al-Hasan explained: {trap}if you do not believe you will be reckoned and recompensed{/trap}, then why do you not return this soul to its body? Mujahid said it means: if you are not certain.
now: You act as if your choices are yours alone, nobody's business. {trap}Answerable to no one.{/trap} But you did not choose to be born, and you cannot choose the day you leave. {idea}You are owned.{/idea}
old: My life is mine; I answer to no one.
new: If I can't keep my soul in my body, I don't fully own my life.
try: Make one decision today by first asking: how would I answer for this?

title: Bring the soul back, if you are telling the truth.
subtitle: The challenge no one has ever met
then: Ibn Kathir explains: {idea}will you not return this soul to its body as it used to be{/idea}, if you are free from reckoning? No one can, and his heading calls this proof that the reckoning will happen.
now: Every hospital in the world, every billionaire, every scientist: {trap}none has brought back a single soul.{/trap} {idea}That limit is a message about who is in charge.{/idea}
old: Humans will figure out how to beat death eventually.
new: No one has returned a soul, which tells me who will judge.
try: Pray one prayer today calmly, with the gentle thought that it could be your last.

title: If the dying person was one of those brought near...
subtitle: The three groups return, at the moment of death
then: Ibn Kathir says these are {idea}the three conditions people face upon their death{/idea}, the same three groups from the surah's opening. Those brought near fulfilled the obligations and the recommended acts, and avoided even some allowed things.
now: The surah began with the end of the world. It ends with the end of one person: someone you know, maybe you. {idea}The same three groups, now in a single bedroom.{/idea}
old: The Day is far away; death is just an ending.
new: Death is the first moment I learn which group I'm in.
try: Do one good act today that is not required: two extra rakat, a charity, a few minutes of dhikr.

title: For them: rest, provision, and a Garden of Delight.
subtitle: The good news given at death
then: Ibn Abbas said Rawh means rest and Rayhan a place of rest; others said mercy, joy and provision. The angels bring {reward}this good news at death{/reward}. The Prophet ﷺ said whoever loves to meet Allah, Allah loves to meet him, and explained that this news is what makes the believer love it.
now: You tense up at funerals and steer away from the topic. {trap}Death feels like only loss.{/trap} {reward}For the believer, it opens with rest and a welcome.{/reward}
old: Death is just loss and darkness.
new: For those near to Allah, death opens with rest and good news.
try: Ask Allah today: make the best of my days the day I meet You.

title: And if the dying one was among the people of the right...
subtitle: The ordinary believer's moment
then: Ibn Kathir describes this as the dying person who is {reward}among those on the right{/reward}, the believers just below the nearest in rank. The surah gives them their own moment, separate from the foremost.
now: You are probably not the most devoted person in your mosque. You try, you fall short, you come back. {reward}The verse sets a moment aside for people like you.{/reward}
old: The beautiful deathbed scenes are for very pious people.
new: Ordinary believers on the right have their own welcome.
try: Keep up one small good habit today that you would love to die upon.

title: Peace to you, you are of the people of the right.
subtitle: The angels' greeting at the last moment
then: Ikrimah said {reward}the angels will greet him with salam{/reward} and tell him he is among those on the right. Ibn Kathir calls this a good explanation and links it to the verse where angels descend saying: fear not, and do not grieve.
now: You wait outside an exam hall, nervous, and a friend comes out smiling: you passed. The relief is everything. {reward}This salam is that, at the end of a whole life.{/reward}
old: My last moments will be full of fear.
new: For the people of the right, the last words heard are peace.
try: Give salam to three people today, fully and warmly.

title: But if he was among the deniers who went astray...
subtitle: The third group, at death

row.title: it can be reversed
sub: while the soul is in the body

then: Ibn Kathir describes them as {trap}those who denied the truth, were led astray from guidance{/trap}, and did not know Allah. The same two words, deniers and astray, were used for the people of the left earlier in the surah.
now: It begins with small choices: ignoring a reminder, mocking someone who prays, telling yourself it is all made up. {idea}While you are alive, every one of those can be reversed.{/idea}
old: Denial is just a personal opinion with no consequences.
new: Denial has an end point, and I can turn back before it.
try: If you have mocked or brushed off faith recently, ask Allah's forgiveness for it today.

title: Their welcome is boiling water.
subtitle: A guest's welcome, turned to punishment
then: The word nuzul, a guest's welcome, appears again. Ibn Kathir says he is received {trap}as a guest, with Hamim{/trap}, boiling water. The near are welcomed with rest. The deniers' welcome is the reverse.
now: You know how it feels to arrive somewhere you are not wanted. {idea}The verse is a warning to make sure you arrive as a welcome guest{/idea}, and there is still time to prepare.
old: I'll worry about the next life later.
new: My welcome there depends on how I live here.
try: Make one sincere tawbah today for something specific.

title: And entry into the blazing Fire.
subtitle: The final end of denial
then: Ibn Kathir says {trap}he will reside in Hellfire{/trap}. The verse is short and sober. It completes the three endings: rest for the near, peace for the right, and this for those who denied.
now: You might feel this verse land on you as you think of things you have done. {idea}That feeling is a mercy, not a sentence.{/idea} {reward}While you breathe, the door of repentance is open.{/reward}
old: I've done too much wrong; this verse is about me.
new: This verse warns me while I can still turn, and that is mercy.
try: Say astaghfirullah wa atubu ilayh sincerely three times today.

title: This is the certain truth.
subtitle: No doubt, no escape, no exception
then: Ibn Kathir says {idea}this news is the truth; there is no doubt about it, nor escape from it for anyone{/idea}. The surah opened by saying no one would deny the Event when it comes. It closes by calling all of it certain.
now: You hold many things as certain: the sunrise, the date your rent is due, that you will get older. {idea}This verse adds one more to that list.{/idea}
old: The afterlife is something I hope is true.
new: The afterlife is as certain as anything I know.
try: Write one sentence about the Day as a certainty and keep it where you will see it.

title: End with praise: glorify your Lord, the Most Great.
subtitle: The surah closes the way the signs closed
then: After the certain truth comes the command: {reward}glorify the name of your Lord, the Most Great{/reward}. The Prophet ﷺ said two phrases are light on the tongue, heavy on the Balance, and loved by the Most Merciful: glory be to Allah and with His praise, glory be to Allah the Magnificent.
now: At a red light, in the lift, waiting for the kettle. Ten seconds you usually give to your phone. {reward}Two light phrases fit there.{/reward}
old: Remembering Allah needs a special time and place.
new: Two short phrases, said anywhere, are heavy on the Balance.
try: Say subhanAllahi wa bihamdihi, subhanAllahil Azim at one red light or queue today.
